facts.text: Nearsightedness (myopia) usually happens when the eyeball grows too long from front to back, so light focuses in front of the retina and faraway objects look blurry.
Nearsightedness usually starts between ages 6 and 14 and gets worse until the early twenties.
Children who spend more time outdoors are less likely to become nearsighted, but experts are not sure why.
Taiwan's school eyesight screening tests the uncorrected vision of all students in grades 1 to 6 every half year.
Among Taiwan's primary school students, the share with reduced vision rose from 34.8 percent in 2001 to 50.0 percent in 2011.
A program called Tian-Tian 120, begun in September 2010, encouraged Taiwanese schools to take students outdoors for 120 minutes every day to prevent myopia.
After Tian-Tian 120 began, the share of Taiwanese primary school students with reduced vision fell every year, from 49.4 percent in 2012 to 46.1 percent in 2015.
In a study at two primary schools in southern Taiwan, one school encouraged children to go outside during class recess and the other made no change.
After 1 year, 8.41 percent of children at the outdoor-recess school had newly developed myopia, compared with 17.65 percent at the other school.
The new-myopia rate at the outdoor-recess school (8.41 percent) was less than half the rate at the other school (17.65 percent).

In Taipei, the share of elementary school students with poor uncorrected eyesight fell from 49.44 percent in the 2014 school year to 43.51 percent in the 2019 school year, then rose to 45.02 percent in 2023 and was 44.35 percent in 2025.
In Taipei, the share of junior high school students with poor uncorrected eyesight was 77.67 percent in the 2014 school year and 72.13 percent in the 2025 school year.

In every Taipei school year from 2014 to 2025, the junior high rate was more than 25 percentage points higher than the elementary school rate; the gap was 32.84 points in 2019 and 27.78 points in 2025.
